spans.assertion: the analysis used data from 146,028 player-referee dyads across four major European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain) for the 2012-2013 season
the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give dark-skinned players red cards than light-skinned players is supported by the data
the estimate adjusts for games played, player position, league, aggressive play style (yellow cards), and referee country bias
dark-skinned players (≥0.75) have a 0.28 percentage point higher probability of red cards than light-skinned players (≤0.25), 95% CI 0.10–0.46 pp, p=0.0023
the adjusted odds ratio is 1.26 (95% CI 1.09–1.46, p=0.0023), i.e. 26% higher odds of red card for dark-skinned players
baseline red card rate for light-skinned players is 1.22%
the 0.28pp increase is a 23% relative increase from baseline
number needed to harm is approximately 357 dyads per one additional red card to a dark-skinned player
the primary estimand was defined as the adjusted percentage-point risk difference in P(red card) between dark and light skin tone
the adjusted risk difference is 0.2802 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0999, 0.4605] pp, p=0.0023 (two-sided, α=0.05), Z=3.045
the result is interpreted as strong evidence against the null hypothesis of no difference, since the CI excludes zero and p is well below 0.05
the secondary estimand was defined as the adjusted odds ratio comparing dark vs light skin tone
the adjusted odds ratio is 1.2602, 95% CI [1.0864, 1.4619], p=0.0023 (two-sided, α=0.05)
the odds of a red card are 26% higher for dark-skinned players, and the CI excludes 1.0 confirming significance
the unit of analysis was chosen as the player-referee dyad
the final analytic sample is 107,489 dyads, comprising 90,040 light-skin (83.8%) and 17,449 dark-skin (16.2%) dyads
the sample includes 1,359 unique players
the sample includes 2,824 unique referees
skin tone was coded by two independent raters from players' profile photos
a 5-point scale (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0 from very light to very dark) was used for skin tone
inter-rater reliability is Pearson r=0.923
"dark skin" was operationalized as an average rater rating ≥0.75
"light skin" was operationalized as an average rater rating ≤0.25
the analysis was restricted to the extreme skin-tone groups for the clearest comparison
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator for any red card in the dyad
overall red card prevalence is 1.25% (1,344 red cards across 107,489 dyads)
log(games played) was included as a covariate for exposure adjustment
player position was included as a categorical covariate
league country was included as a categorical covariate
standardized yellow-card count was included as a covariate, as a proxy for aggressive play style
standardized mean referee-country implicit bias (race IAT) was included as a covariate
standardized mean referee-country explicit bias (racial thermometer) was included as a covariate
the analysis started with 146,028 total player-referee dyads
21,407 dyads missing skin-tone ratings (no photo) were excluded
the sample was restricted to light/dark skin-tone extremes, yielding 107,606 dyads
117 dyads with missing covariate data (primarily referee bias measures) were excluded
final sample is 107,489 dyads (73.6% of the original)
logistic regression was used as the model
the model was estimated via maximum likelihood using statsmodels v0.14+
robust (sandwich-estimator) standard errors were used
standard errors were not clustered
average marginal effects were calculated using numerical derivatives
a Wald test with normal approximation was used for two-sided inference
model fit statistics: pseudo R² (McFadden)=0.091, log-likelihood=-6567.0, AIC=13,160, likelihood-ratio test p<0.001
standard errors were not clustered by player or referee
the resulting bias from not clustering is judged likely modest given the large number of clusters and balanced design
player or referee fixed effects were not included
this limitation is judged to be mitigated by controlling for aggressive play and implicit/explicit referee bias
dyads were not weighted by number of games played (all weighted equally)
the lack of weighting is addressed by including log(games) as a covariate
the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players is SUPPORTED by the data
the effect is in the hypothesized direction (positive association between dark skin and red cards)
the 0.28pp difference is small in absolute terms but a 23% relative increase from the 1.22% baseline
p=0.0023, well below α=0.05
the 95% CI [0.10, 0.46] excludes zero with substantial margin
the effect is consistent across minimal, medium, and full covariate specifications, with risk differences ranging 0.25–0.28 pp
a dose-response analysis was run using continuous skin tone across all players rather than only the extremes
a 0.35 percentage point increase per 1-unit increase in continuous skin tone was found (p=0.003)

spans.note: restates that the modest effect is meaningful in context

spans.assertion: because red cards are rare, even small absolute changes represent substantial relative increases
over a career with many referee encounters, the cumulative disadvantage to dark-skinned players could be appreciable
the effect persists after controlling for aggressive play (yellow cards), suggesting it is not explained by behavioral differences
14.7% of dyads were excluded due to missing skin-tone ratings (no photo)
missing photos are judged more likely related to player prominence/club resources, partially controlled for via the league covariate
restricting to extreme skin tones excluded 31% of rated dyads with medium skin tone
this restriction is judged to improve interpretability but may not generalize to medium skin tones

spans.note: generic caveat that yellow cards may not fully capture play style, leaving possible residual confounding

spans.assertion: player reputation was not controlled for, though it may influence referee decisions
individual referee characteristics (experience, age, own race/ethnicity) were not controlled for, only referee country-level bias
match context (score differential, home/away status, match importance) was not controlled for
skin tone coded from static photos may not reflect in-game appearance (lighting, uniforms, distance)
raters were kept blind to the hypothesis to reduce motivated bias
high inter-rater reliability (r=0.923) is judged to indicate the skin-tone measurement is reliable
red-card records are assumed accurate and unlikely to be systematically misclassified by skin tone
standard errors were not clustered despite non-independent observations within player/referee
this is judged to likely underestimate uncertainty but cushioned by the large number of clusters and the significance level
robustness of results to covariate specification was tested, though functional-form misspecification cannot be fully ruled out
whether the skin-tone effect varies by league, position, or referee bias was not tested

spans.note: states the assumption being evaluated: exposure adequately controls for opportunity to receive a red card

a log transformation of games played was used to account for diminishing returns

spans.note: states the assumption being evaluated: included covariates adequately control for confounding

spans.note: states the assumption being evaluated: no substantial violation of logistic regression assumptions

spans.assertion: this assumption is assessed as largely met (binary outcome, large sample n>100,000, model converged)
non-independence of observations within player/referee was not fully addressed

spans.assertion: the MAR assumption is assessed as uncertain, since missingness is plausibly related to player prominence/club resources
complete-case analysis was used for missing data, acknowledged as standard but not ideal
a sensitivity analysis was run using continuous skin tone across all players instead of only the extreme groups
a similar effect was found in that analysis (0.35 pp per unit, p=0.003)
covariate specifications ranging from minimal (games only) to full were tested
the effect was found consistent across specifications, 0.25pp (minimal) vs 0.28pp (full)
data quality was checked via inter-rater reliability and within-player consistency of skin-tone ratings across dyads
inter-rater reliability was found high and skin tone consistent within players across dyads
standard errors were not clustered by player or referee
interactions (effect modification) were not tested
causal effects were not estimated using propensity scores, instrumental variables, or sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding (e.g. E-value)
results are from the 2012-2013 season across 4 European leagues and may not generalize to other times, leagues, or sports
all code is provided in final_analysis.py and the analysis is fully reproducible from the raw data file
a binary skin-tone definition (dark ≥0.75 vs light ≤0.25) was chosen specifically to maximize contrast
sensitivity analysis confirmed similar results using the continuous skin-tone measure
covariate selection was guided by DAG reasoning, including confounders (position, league, exposure) and mediators to control (yellow cards, referee bias)
complete-case analysis (listwise deletion) was used for missing data for simplicity, excluding 117 observations (0.1%)
pseudo-R² is modest (0.09) but deemed expected for a rare binary outcome; model converged without issue

overall conclusion: strong evidence referees issue more red cards to dark-skinned players even after adjustment; risk difference 0.28pp (CI 0.10–0.46, p=0.0023), 23% relative increase; significant, consistent, and robust
the cumulative effect over many referee encounters across a career could meaningfully disadvantage dark-skinned players
limitations reiterated: potential unmeasured confounding (player reputation, match context), lack of clustered standard errors, restriction to one season across four leagues
future research should examine mechanisms, test effect modification, and extend to other contexts, implying these were not done here
final determination: hypothesis SUPPORTED
unadjusted red-card rate is 1.22% for light-skinned players vs 1.42% for dark-skinned players
